hops.afterHeading: Explain: particles spread from more to less
hops.title: How a smell really crosses a room
hops.text: Spray perfume in one corner, and someone across the room smells it within seconds. Diffusion usually gets the credit, but it is too slow for that trip. In still air, diffusion alone could take about a day to spread some perfume ingredients a meter. Moving air does most of the carrying. Diffusion helps spread the scent too, and it crosses the last tiny gap at the lining of the nose.

hops.afterHeading: Explain: water crosses a choosy membrane
hops.title: Why seawater makes a thirsty person thirstier
hops.text: Lost at sea, a person has water everywhere and none to drink. Human kidneys cannot make urine as salty as seawater. So clearing the salt from a drink takes more water than the drink provided. Drink enough, and the blood gets saltier than the liquid inside the body's cells. Cell membranes hold most of that salt back, so water drifts out, the same way it leaves a salted cucumber.

hops.title: Soak raisins and compare them with a dry one
hops.text: A raisin is a dried grape packed with sugar. Its skin lets water through. Put a few in a clear glass of plain water and keep one dry beside it. After a day, compare a soaked raisin with the dry one. What difference do you see? Which way did the water move, and what did the sugar have to do with it? Throw the soaked ones away without tasting them.

audio.title: Three real-world stories about water on the move
audio.transcript:
Let's take a quick trip through three real-world stories about water. Two of them show the same quiet rule at work. The third shows why it pays to check the evidence before you give that rule the credit.

Our first stop is Paris, almost three hundred years ago. A scientist named Jean Antoine Nollet has a vessel of alcohol, and he covers it with a very unusual lid. A piece of pig bladder. Yes, really! He sets the whole thing in a bigger container of water, and then he waits.

Nobody squeezes anything. Nobody pumps anything. And yet the bladder starts to puff up! Water from the outside gets through it more easily than the alcohol gets out. More water comes in, and more, and more. The bladder stretches tight. When Nollet pricks it with a pin, a jet of liquid shoots up more than a foot!

So the thin layer lets the water pass, and the difference between the two liquids sets the direction. More water crosses one way than the other, with no pump at all. Here is the best part. Every cell in your body is wrapped in a membrane that is choosy in its own way. That old pig bladder has a lot to do with you.

For our second stop, imagine a small boat on the open ocean. The people on board are very thirsty. There is water in every direction, and all of it is salty. Drinking it seems like it ought to help. It does not!

Here is the trouble. Human kidneys can only make urine that is less salty than seawater. So to get rid of the salt from seawater, the body has to pass more water than the person drank. The more seawater someone drinks, the further behind they fall.

Then comes a second problem. When the blood gets saltier than the liquid inside cells, and the cell membranes hold most of that salt back, water drifts out of the cells. Even cells in the brain can shrink. It is the same drift that pulls water out of a salted cucumber, only now it is happening inside a person. So the body loses water getting rid of the salt, and the cells lose water to the salty blood. That is how someone can be surrounded by water and still become dangerously dehydrated, even while feeling thirstier.

Our last stop is much closer to home. It is your bathtub! Stay in long enough and your fingertips go wrinkly. The answer seems easy. Water must be soaking into your skin and puffing it up. Good guess! But almost a hundred years ago, two researchers described something odd. When a nerve in the hand was damaged, the skin served by that nerve did not get those wrinkles.

Wait a minute. If wrinkles were only water soaking in, a damaged nerve should make no difference. So what was going on? Later studies found the answer. Your nervous system narrows the blood vessels in your fingertips. The soft pad of each finger gets pulled inward a little, and the skin on top folds. Your body is actively making those wrinkles!

What are they for? That is still an open question. One study found that people with wrinkled fingers moved wet objects faster. A later, larger study could not find that advantage. Scientists are still sorting it out. So the next time you look down at your fingers in the tub, give them a wiggle. You are looking at a question nobody has fully answered yet.
